slides.title: Building Sentences
slides.subtitle: Lesson 10 · Simple, Compound & Complex · the Interjection

slides.text: A Simple Sentence consists of a single proposition.
examples: Ellen and Mary study botany.  (compound subject — still one proposition)

slides.heading: Combining Sentences
bullets: “I see a dog.”  “I see a boy.”  “I see a tree.”  “I see a house.” — *I see* is a part common to all of them.
Use the common part but once, and the four become a single sentence:  “I see a dog, a boy, a tree, and a house.”

slides.heading: Practice — Combining (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Combine the sentences in each group into a single sentence.
items: I found a book. I found a pencil. I found a slate. I found a knife.
John walked to the lake. John walked over the hill. John walked rapidly.
The horse was old. The horse was lame. The horse was blind.
answers: I found a book, a pencil, a slate, and a knife.
John walked rapidly over the hill to the lake.
The horse was old, lame, and blind.

slides.heading: Practice — Combining (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Combine the sentences in each group into a single sentence.
items: Apple trees grow thriftily. Apple trees grow in our orchard.
The wind blew fiercely. The wind blew last night. The wind blew from the north.
William gave me a new book. William sold me ten marbles. William bought a sled for my brother.
answers: Apple trees grow thriftily in our orchard.
The wind blew fiercely from the north last night.
William gave me a new book, sold me ten marbles, and bought a sled for my brother.

slides.text: A Compound Sentence consists of two or more connected sentences, each of which will make complete sense when standing alone.
examples: Wheat grows in the field, **and** men reap it.
The wind blew, **but** the ship was safe.
He is at home, **or** he is at school.

slides.heading: Members & Common Parts
bullets: Rem. — The sentences of which a compound sentence is composed are called *Members*.
“Exercise strengthens the constitution, and temperance strengthens the constitution.” — *exercise* and *temperance* are the parts not common to the two members.
Unite the parts not common, and use the common parts but once:  “Exercise and temperance strengthen the constitution” — a simple sentence.

slides.heading: Practice — Change to Simple (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Change each compound sentence to a simple one.
items: Behold my mother, and behold my brethren.
I saw a man in a boat, and I saw a boy in the water.
Washington was a warrior, and Washington was a statesman.
answers: Behold my mother and my brethren.
I saw a man in a boat and a boy in the water.
Washington was a warrior and a statesman.

slides.heading: Practice — Change to Simple (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Change each compound sentence to a simple one.
items: The man you saw was sick, or he was in trouble.
The river was swift, and it was very deep.
answers: The man you saw was sick or in trouble.  (*you saw* is still an adjective clause)
The river was swift and very deep.

rows.sentence: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament showeth his handiwork.
rows.note: Declarative; compound. *The heavens declare the glory of God* is the first member;  *the firmament showeth his handiwork*, the second;  *and*, the connective.  *heavens* is the subject of the first member;  *declare*, the predicate, modified by *glory*, an objective element, which *the* and the phrase *of God* modify.  *firmament* is the subject of the second;  *showeth* (= shows), the predicate, modified by *handiwork*, an objective element, which *his* modifies.

slides.heading: Practice — Members (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Name the members of each compound sentence and the connective.
items: Talent is something, but tact is every thing.
Art is long, and time is fleeting.
Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.
The stores were closed, and the hum of business was hushed.
answers: Talent is something · tact is every thing — *but*
Art is long · time is fleeting — *and*
Lead us not into temptation · deliver us from evil — *but*
The stores were closed · the hum of business was hushed — *and*

slides.heading: Practice — Members (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Name the members of each compound sentence and the connective.
items: Every eye was filled with tears, and, for a moment, all were silent.
You may stay here with me, or we will go to the lecture with Susan.
The gathering clouds threatened an approaching storm, and the deep darkness of the night soon enveloped them.
answers: Every eye was filled with tears · for a moment, all were silent — *and*
You may stay here with me · we will go to the lecture with Susan — *or*
The gathering clouds threatened an approaching storm · the deep darkness of the night soon enveloped them — *and*

slides.heading: Members & Truth
bullets: Each member of a declarative compound sentence is a proposition, true or false by itself.  (A command — *Lead us not…* — is neither.)
*and*, *but* — both members are affirmed:  true if both are true;  false if either is false.  *but* adds contrast, not a different truth.
*or* — true if at least one member is true;  false only if neither is.
*either…or* — true if exactly one member is true;  false if neither is, or both are.

slides.text: A Complex Sentence is one some element of which contains a subject and a predicate.
examples: The house **that Jack built** is old.

slides.heading: Principal & Subordinate Clauses
bullets: A clause must contain a subject and a predicate.
“I know where gold is found.” — *I know* makes complete sense standing alone:  the *Principal Clause*.  *where gold is found* does not:  a *Subordinate Clause*.
A Principal Clause is one which makes complete sense when separated from the rest of the sentence.
A Subordinate Clause is one which does not make complete sense when separated from the rest of the sentence.

rows.label: Subject
rows.text: A clause used as the subject.
rows.examples: “Haste makes waste,” is a true saying.

rows.label: Predicate
rows.text: A clause used as the predicate.
rows.examples: My hope is, that he will recover.

rows.label: Objective
rows.text: A clause used as an objective element.
rows.examples: I believe that the earth is round.

rows.label: Adjective
rows.text: A clause used as an adjective element.
rows.examples: The report that he is insane, is unfounded.

rows.label: Adverbial
rows.text: A clause used as an adverbial element.
rows.examples: Our teacher is delighted when we are studious.

slides.heading: Remarks on Analysis
bullets: Rem. 1. — A complex sentence whose subject or predicate only is a clause need not be separated into principal and subordinate clauses.
Rem. 2. — Some complex sentences are composed of many clauses.  Each clause should be analyzed in the order indicated by its position.

rows.sentence: He that hateth, dissembleth with his lips.
rows.note: Declarative; complex.  *He dissembleth with his lips* is the principal clause;  *that hateth*, the subordinate clause, an adjective element modifying *He*.  Of the clause, *that* is the subject;  *hateth*, the predicate.  *dissembleth* is modified by the phrase *with his lips*, an adverbial element;  *lips*, by *his*.  (*hateth* = hates;  *dissembleth* = disguises the truth)

rows.sentence: He builds a palace of ice where the torrents fall.
rows.note: Declarative; complex.  *He builds a palace of ice* is the principal clause;  *the torrents fall*, the subordinate clause;  *where*, the connective.  *builds* is modified by *palace*, an objective element, which *a* and the phrase *of ice* modify, and by the clause *where the torrents fall*, an adverbial element.  *torrents* is modified by *the*;  *fall*, by *where*.

rows.sentence: That he is very sick, is evident.
rows.note: Declarative; complex;  its subject is a clause.  *That he is very sick* is the subject;  *evident*, the predicate;  *is*, the copula.  In the subject clause, *he* is the subject;  *sick*, the predicate, modified by *very*;  *is*, the copula.  *That* is a conjunction introducing the clause.

rows.sentence: He never denied that the letter was lost.
rows.note: Declarative; complex.  *He never denied* is the principal clause;  *the letter was lost*, the subordinate clause;  *that*, the connective.  *denied* is modified by *never*, an adverbial element, and by the clause *that the letter was lost*, an objective element.

slides.heading: Clauses & Truth
bullets: A subordinate clause is a proposition used as an element:  it is not affirmed on its own, as a member is.
“He never denied that the letter was lost.” — true or false whether or not the letter was lost.
“That he is very sick, is evident.” — *evident* is affirmed of a whole proposition:  *he is very sick*.

slides.heading: Practice — Subordinate Clauses (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Name the subordinate clause and tell its class.
items: He that flattereth, deceiveth his neighbor.
The boy that you saw, is my younger brother.
He was frightened when he first saw a lion.
I can not study where pupils make so much noise.
answers: that flattereth — adjective
that you saw — adjective
when he first saw a lion — adverbial
where pupils make so much noise — adverbial

slides.heading: Practice — Subordinate Clauses (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Name the subordinate clause and tell its class.  If the subject only is a clause, say so (Rem. 1).
items: I would pay you if I had the money.
That he will succeed, is uncertain.
The messenger reported that the brave general was dead.
He is a good man, though very eccentric.
answers: if I had the money — adverbial
That he will succeed — subject clause  (Rem. 1:  need not be separated)
that the brave general was dead — objective
though [he is] very eccentric — adverbial

slides.heading: Practice — Subordinate Clauses (Set 3)
slides.instruction: Name every subordinate clause and tell its class.
items: Nature never did betray the heart that loved her.
The poor too often turn away, unheard, / From hearts that shut against them, with a sound / That shall be heard in heaven.  — Longfellow
answers: that loved her — adjective
that shut against them — adjective (modifies *hearts*);  That shall be heard in heaven — adjective (modifies *sound*)

slides.heading: Reducing & Enlarging
bullets: Complex sentences may often be reduced to simple sentences by using single words or phrases, instead of subordinate propositions, as modifiers.
“A man who is wealthy, lives there” = “A man of wealth lives there,” or “A wealthy man lives there.”
Simple sentences may often be enlarged to complex sentences by using subordinate propositions, instead of single words or phrases, as modifiers.
“None think the great unhappy but the great” = “None think that the great are unhappy but the great.”

slides.heading: Practice — Reduce to Simple (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Reduce each complex sentence to a simple sentence.  Model — “We started when the sun rose” = “We started at sunrise.”
items: A pupil that is studious, will learn rapidly.
Men who are honest, are respected.
A boy, when he is at play, is happy.
An accident that was unavoidable, occurred at the factory this morning.
answers: A studious pupil will learn rapidly.
Honest men are respected.
A boy at play is happy.
An unavoidable accident occurred at the factory this morning.

slides.heading: Practice — Reduce to Simple (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Reduce each complex sentence to a simple sentence.
items: Franklin, who was a philosopher, was an American.
One soldier was not present when the roll was called.
They weighed anchor when the tide turned.
My brother has gone to the city that he may find employment.
answers: Franklin, a philosopher, was an American.
One soldier was not present at roll call.
They weighed anchor at the turn of the tide.
My brother has gone to the city to find employment.

slides.heading: Practice — Enlarge to Complex (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Enlarge each simple sentence to a complex sentence, using a clause instead of the marked words.
items: A thing **of beauty** is a joy forever.
I went down to the river **at ten o’clock**.
Thou hast uttered **cruel** words.
The poor must work **in their grief**.
answers: A thing that is beautiful is a joy forever.
I went down to the river when it was ten o’clock.
Thou hast uttered words that are cruel.
The poor must work while they grieve.

slides.heading: Practice — Enlarge to Complex (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Enlarge each simple sentence to a complex sentence, using a clause instead of the marked words.
items: Time **wasted** is existence;  **used**, is life.
They came here **to see the country**.
The wild beasts **kept for the games**, had broken from their dens.
Haste **to cheer my father’s heart**.
answers: Time that is wasted is existence;  time that is used is life.
They came here that they might see the country.
The wild beasts that were kept for the games, had broken from their dens.
Haste, that thou mayest cheer my father’s heart.

slides.heading: Practice — Which Kind?
slides.instruction: Name the kind of each sentence.
items: Iron and lead are heavy.
The sun rose, and the mist vanished.
The tree that fell was an oak.
We waited until noon.
We waited until he came.
He is poor, but he is honest.
He said that the road was closed.
Eli ran, jumped, and shouted.
answers: simple
compound
complex
simple
complex
compound
complex
simple

slides.heading: Oral Lesson — the Interjection
bullets: “Hurra! we have found him.” — *we* is the subject;  *have found*, the predicate, modified by *him*, an objective element.
What does *hurra* denote?  That the speaker is highly pleased.  Does it affirm or deny any thing?  It does not:  it simply implies a feeling of pleasure.
Other words denote sorrow, grief, surprise, disgust, pity, hatred.  All such words are called *Interjections*.

slides.text: An Interjection is a word used to denote some sudden or strong emotion.

slides.heading: Remarks on the Interjection
bullets: Rem. — Interjections usually, but not always, require an exclamation point [ ! ] after them.
An interjection is no part of the proposition:  “Alas! the ship was lost” is true just when the ship was lost.
Note. — Interjections may be omitted in analysis.  In a diagram they may be placed before and a little above the first words.

rows.note: Declarative.  *we* is the subject;  *have found*, the predicate, modified by *him*, an objective element.  *Hurra* is an interjection;  it denotes pleasure.
Declarative.  *they* is the subject;  *are coming*, the predicate.  *Hush* is an interjection;  it denotes some sudden emotion.

slides.heading: Practice — Interjections (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Point out the interjection in each sentence.
items: Ha! it freezes me.
Aha! you are a truant.
Ahem! I will think about it.
Hark! the clock strikes one.
Pshaw! I knew that yesterday.
Alas! we shall see him no more.
answers: Ha
Aha
Ahem
Hark
Pshaw
Alas

slides.heading: Practice — Interjections (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Point out the interjections in each sentence.
items: Tush! tush! man, I made no reference to you.
Ay, he is every inch a king.
Oh, what a noble mind is here o’erthrown!  (*o’erthrown* = overthrown)
Alas! they had been friends in youth.
Hark! hark! the lark at heaven’s gate sings.
Alas! for the rarity of Christian charity.
answers: Tush, tush
Ay  (= yes)
Oh
Alas
Hark, hark
Alas

slides.heading: Practice — Parts of Speech (Set 1)
slides.instruction: Point out all the parts of speech in each sentence.
items: Ha! it freezes me.
Aha! you are a truant.
Alas! they had been friends in youth.
Alas! we shall see him no more.
answers: Ha — interjection;  it — pronoun;  freezes — verb;  me — pronoun
Aha — interjection;  you — pronoun;  are — verb;  a — adjective (article);  truant — noun
Alas — interjection;  they — pronoun;  had been — verb;  friends — noun;  in — preposition;  youth — noun
Alas — interjection;  we — pronoun;  shall see — verb;  him — pronoun;  no, more — adverbs

slides.heading: Practice — Parts of Speech (Set 2)
slides.instruction: Point out all the parts of speech in each sentence.
items: Ahem! I will think about it.
Hark! hark! the lark at heaven’s gate sings.
Tush! tush! man, I made no reference to you.
Alas! for the rarity of Christian charity.
answers: Ahem — interjection;  I — pronoun;  will think — verb;  about — preposition;  it — pronoun
Hark, hark — interjections;  the — adjective (article);  lark — noun;  at — preposition;  heaven’s — noun;  gate — noun;  sings — verb
Tush, tush — interjections;  man — noun;  I — pronoun;  made — verb;  no — adjective;  reference — noun;  to — preposition;  you — pronoun
Alas — interjection;  for — preposition;  the — adjective (article);  rarity — noun;  of — preposition;  Christian — adjective;  charity — noun

slides.heading: The Eight Parts of Speech
bullets: Noun — a name.
Pronoun — used instead of a noun.
Verb — expresses action, being, or state.
Adjective — describes or defines a noun.
Adverb — modifies a verb, an adjective, a participle, or an adverb.
Preposition — shows the relation between its object and some other word.
Conjunction — connects words, phrases, clauses, and members.
Interjection — denotes some sudden or strong emotion.
